chapters.title: Getting the Right Perspective towards Investing
chapters.summary:
Vijay Malik opens with a confession: his portfolio became his alternative income dream, echoing Warren Buffett's Berkshire where operating profits feed the parent, yet his early journey chased emotion. The perspective chapter defines investing as hard work over hard dreaming, a mantra repeated when he cites Jeanne Sahadi on missing the ten best months. An illustration replicates the missing best months table where missing ten high-return months over thirty years cuts returns from 11.5 to 5.8 percent, proving that timing destroys the dream. Malik stresses the behavioral finance lens: fear, greed, and frustration cause premature selling when prices rise and panic when they fall, turning a dream portfolio into a trading diary.

The anecdote that anchors this is his own first market foray without perspective, buying on tips and celebrating early gains that reversed. The illustration shows a disposition effect chart where investors sell winners early and ride losers. The chapter's toolkit is perspective as process: write down why you bought, what would make you sell, and how many hours of research back each position, a one-page perspective sheet reproduced. The authorship note about communicating via drvijaymalik.com frames the book as a practitioner's notes, not theory, with page footers reminding copyright and site. The key framework is investor versus trader perspective: investor asks can this business sustain returns through cycles with promoter integrity, trader asks will price move next month.

Malik insists that portfolio management is passion not job, quoting Buffett at 84 saying loving your job ensures longevity, but clarifies that passion means reading footnotes not watching tickers. The closing checklist asks readers to reframe every tip as perspective test: does the pitch survive a three-year hold thought experiment where market shuts tomorrow? If not, it is speculation masquerading as investing. The illustration of two roads — patience lane compounding versus timing lane whipsawing — sets the visual motif for the entire book where peace comes from perspective that outlasts price. The chapter supplements the narrative with charts, fieldwork photographs, and peer comparison tables that ground every claim in primary data and let readers replicate the screen on their own portfolios.

chapters.title: Choosing the Stock Picking Approach Suitable to You
chapters.summary:
Malik argues stock picking style must fit your personality, calendar, and competence circle, not guru fashion. He catalogs three archetypes: deep value Ben Graham cigar butt buying net-nets, growth at reasonable price à la Phil Fisher and Peter Lynch buying visible earnings compounding, and quality at any price that chases moats. A comparison table illustrates each on time needed per company, turnover, drawdown tolerance, and typical mistake — value traps, growth traps, and valuation traps. His own migration from technical analysis to value is previewed but not yet detailed, with a chart showing his early technical trades where win rate was high but position size wrong, eroding expectancy.

The anecdote is his attempt to mimic a friend's momentum system that required daily screen time he lacked as a doctor, leading to missed signals and losses, proving approach must match lifestyle. The illustration overlays two equity curves: trader's jagged high turnover versus investor's smooth low turnover after costs. The framework introduced is the confidence circle: list industries you understand enough to explain cash flow in one page. Malik's own circle excludes banks initially because he could not distinguish solvency from liquidity, a humility he later revisits.

The checklist for choosing approach asks four questions: how many hours weekly can you research, can you stomach a fifty percent paper loss on a correctly picked compounder for two years, do you enjoy reading footnotes more than charts, and will your family tolerate boredom. The answer sorts readers into value, GARP, or passive. The chapter's core illustration is a Venn diagram where circle one is competence, circle two is temperament, circle three is time, and the overlap is your sustainable approach; chasing outside the overlap ensures peaceful investing becomes sleepless trading.

The closing note stresses there is no universal best approach, only the one you can execute without abandoning after a bad year, a point reinforced by a churn case where switching styles after one year's underperformance locks in losses. Stay in overlap of competence, temperament, and time where execution survives a bad year.

chapters.title: Why I Left Technical Analysis and Never Returned
chapters.summary:
Malik's breakup with technical analysis is both personal and forensic, and it motivates the fundamental checklists that dominate later chapters. He recounts years drawing trendlines, RSI, and MACD where patterns felt predictive because recent wins were vivid and losses were rationalized as not following the system strictly, an availability bias loop illustrated with a P&L histogram where small wins clustered and rare large stops erased them. The epiphany came from expectancy math: even with sixty percent win rate, poor position sizing and arbitrary stops produced negative expectancy, a table shows entry, stop, target, and realized R multiples where average winner was 0.8 R and loser 1.2 R. An illustration replicates a classic head-and-shoulders that failed, with volume not confirming — the same chart that textbooks label textbook.

Malik then dismantles the claim that price discounts everything, arguing that price discounts expectations, not solvency, and that balance sheet frauds like Satyam showed price trending up while cash was missing, a chart juxtaposes Satyam price rising while CFO cash flow diverged for six quarters before collapse. The anecdote that broke him was buying a stock on breakout, booking twenty percent, watching it triple afterward while he sat out, while another breakout stopped his capital before reversal — the disposition effect amplified by technicals. He quotes Lynch and Buffett on why he shifted: if you can explain earnings, you can hold through volatility; if you explain only price shape, you have nothing to hold.

The chapter's illustration of two investors holding the same stock — fundamentalist calm during fifty percent dip because thesis intact versus technician stopped at ten percent — drives home why peaceful investing needs business understanding not pattern recognition. He does not demonize traders who have systems with positive expectancy and time, but argues that for retail investors seeking alternative income, fundamental analysis allows peace because businesses compound while patterns decay. The closing checklist asks readers to audit any system for expectancy, maximum drawdown, and hours required, and to walk away if expectancy is not calculated on at least one hundred trades, a discipline most chart platforms never enforce.

Hold business thesis through fifty percent dips; pattern stops force selling that forfeits compounding.
Audit any system on 100 trades for expectancy and max drawdown before trusting it with capital.

chapters.title: Shortlisting Companies for Detailed Analysis
chapters.summary:
Shortlisting is triage, not picking, and Malik turns it into a checklist sieve to reduce 5,000 listed firms to a watchlist of fifty without reading full reports. The chapter lists filters he uses on screener.in: market cap above Rs 500 crore to avoid illiquidity where impact cost exceeds edge, debt-equity below 1.0 to filter leverage traps like infrastructure lenders before detailed solvency checks, ROCE above fifteen percent three-year average to keep only those who earn above cost of capital, and promoter pledge below fifty percent to avoid distress risk, illustrated as a funnel diagram where each filter slices the universe.

An anecdote recounts how early in his career he read every annual report alphabetically, wasting months on textile mills with four percent ROCE that never passed later tests, versus now screening first. The famous self-sustainable growth rate is introduced here as g equals ROCE multiplied by retention where retention is one minus payout; if sales growth exceeds g for three years consecutively, leverage is funding growth, a warning. A table shows two firms both growing twenty percent: firm A at twenty-five percent ROCE can self-fund at g of fifteen percent, so gap of five points is debt; firm B at ten percent ROCE with g five needs even more leverage — both flagged. The illustration of sales versus g gap as red flags is the book's most photocopied page.

Malik also filters on cash conversion cycle via working capital days versus peers — if a firm needs ninety days where industry needs thirty, it is either aggressive revenue recognition or inefficient — and on promoter salary versus net profit trend. The chapter includes a live example screening for 2015 where filters yielded Page and Astral early, before they became consensus, a backtest chart shows filtered universe outperforming Sensex by eight percent annually before detailed analysis even begins. For readers who prefer not to screen, he offers an alternative: follow credit rating upgrades where agencies pre-screen solvency, but warns that ratings lag.

The closing note stresses that shortlisting is not buying; it merely orders work so limited research hours focus on businesses with prima facie quality, leaving the forensic seven-signs and valuation sections to kill most survivors anyway. Peace is preserved because you ignore 4,900 firms by rule, reducing envy-driven chasing. chapters.title: How to Conduct Detailed Analysis of a Company
chapters.summary:
Detailed analysis is sequential: business, financial, valuation, and management, summarized in the book's roadmap illustration that the authors suggest printing. Malik insists on business first before numbers because business answers whether numbers can be durable. The chapter structures business analysis into five lenses: does the product solve a real problem customers will pay for repeatedly, is demand unorganized to organized where branding can capture share, does the firm control a bottleneck like distribution or technology, can promoters be trusted to allocate capital, and is the tailwind cyclical or secular. An anecdote dissects a capital goods firm he liked for ROCE until business checks revealed one customer at forty percent of sales, a concentration table shows revenue by client, and he passed because single-client risk dwarfs ratio averages.

Another case contrasts Marico's farmer procurement with a trader-dependent peer where architecture was absent, predicting the latter's margin collapse. The illustration that anchors the chapter is a one-page business canvas with boxes for customer, problem, alternative, moat, and promoter test, completed for Asian Paints as demo. Financial analysis is previewed as self-sustainable growth consistency, free cash flow conversion where CFO should exceed PAT over five years — a CFO versus PAT divergence chart flags Satyam-like gaps — and operating leverage where fixed costs should not outrun volume. Valuation is not price-earnings alone but earnings yield versus cost of capital and growth.

Management assessment is framed as most critical, with later sections allocating three full chapters to it, and an early warning table lists promoter actions that fail it instantly: frequent related-party loans, equity pledges to fund personal ventures, and auditor changes two years consecutively. The detailed analysis workflow ends with final checklist for buying stocks where every prior filter must be green — the book's page 181 checklist is previewed as thumbnail. The closing discipline is time budgeting: two hours to screen, six hours to read annual report and credit report, two hours to value — ten hours per company — so covering fifty firms is a year of weekends, a calendar illustration shows realistic throughput of two companies per week.

This pacing is intentional to prevent tip-driven rushing that skips business diligence. chapters.title: Understanding the Annual Report of a Company
chapters.summary:
Malik walks through the annual report as a detective story where management discussion is claims and notes to accounts are evidence. He advises reading auditor's report and notes first, not the chairman's glossy letter, because auditors disclose related-party transactions, contingent liabilities, and change in accounting policy that letter omits. The chapter annotates a real 2014 annual report excerpt of a mid-cap manufacturer where revenue grew thirty percent but trade receivables grew sixty percent, illustrated as diverging lines, and auditor note revealed extended channel financing to related distributors — a red flag.

Key sections are explained: balance sheet reveals leverage and working capital days where inventory plus receivables minus payables divided by sales times 365 should be stable; profit and loss reveals operating leverage and other income quality — if other income exceeds twenty percent of PBT, earnings are not operating; cash flow reveals whether profits convert to cash, an illustration shows three companies with same profit but cash from operations at 120, 80, and 40 percent of profit, only the first trusted. Related-party section is highlighted as most read: a table lists transactions where promoter entity leased property to company at three times market rent, a governance deduction. Contingent liabilities footnote is decoded: bank guarantees at fifty percent of net worth mean off-balance leverage.

The anecdote is Malik catching a firm capitalizing operating expenses as intangible assets, boosting profit while cash flow lagged, illustrated with asset schedule where intangible jumps without product launch. He also decodes segment reporting where a conglomerate hid loss-making division inside others, and shareholding pattern where promoter holding fell while pledge rose — a divergence chart. The chapter ends with a reading order illustration: start with auditor qualification, then related party, contingent liability, accounting policy changes, then management discussion with skepticism, then financials with five-year trend. The closing tip is to print the report and annotate margins with red flags, building a personal database of promoter language patterns — e.g., we are confident versus we have tied up orders — that later management assessment chapters systematize.

chapters.title: How to Do Financial Analysis of a Company
chapters.summary:
Financial analysis translates business hunches into arithmetic that cannot be faked for long. Malik builds a five-year spreadsheet for each survivor with ROCE, ROE, debt-equity, interest coverage, fixed asset turnover, and cash conversion, illustrated as a single-page dashboard where green stays green for five years, not one. The centrepiece is ratio triangulation: if ROCE is high but CFO lag, earnings are paper; if ROE is high but leverage is high, DuPont breaks to show risk, a DuPont tree decomposes ROE into margin times turnover times leverage, showing Marico's ROE of twenty-five at low leverage versus infrastructure firm's same ROE at high leverage.

The chapter details operating performance steps: sales growth should be volume plus price not just price where volumes stall, shown by decomposing quantity versus rate; operating margin should be stable within three points across cycle, a margin band chart shows Asian Paints narrow versus commodity players wide; asset turnover should rise with scale, a plant utilization curve shows TCS rising while textile mills flat. Inventory and receivables are dissected with days calculations and peer comparison — if a firm's receivable days are twice industry, it is likely funding distributor sales. An anecdote revisits a 2012 pharma pick where ROCE looked great until Malik checked that other income from forex gains comprised thirty percent of profit, and when rupee reversed, profit collapsed, illustrated as forex adjustment line.

The chapter also introduces free cash flow where FCF equals CFO minus maintenance capex not total capex, and owner earnings where growth capex is separated, showing that Page's owner earnings exceed PAT because working capital is negative. The illustration compares FCF yield to earnings yield where a manufacturer with high earnings but zero FCF is flagged. The closing synthesis is the growth sustainability equation revisited: compare sales growth to self-sustainable growth and to FCF; if sales outruns both for two years, the firm is borrowing to grow, a risk that kills peaceful holding. Malik insists financial analysis is not to predict price but to describe durability, and that a five-year consistent dashboard matters more than one-year spike that annual report cherry-picks.

chapters.title: Seven Signs to Tell Whether a Company Is Cooking Its Books
chapters.summary:
The seven financial shenanigans are the book's forensic core, each with a real case anatomy and illustration. Sign one is overstated revenue via channel stuffing where receivables balloon faster than sales, shown with a divergence chart and the 2009 Satyam disclosure where claimed cash lacked bank confirmation. Sign two is understated expenses via capitalizing operating costs as intangible or deferring them, illustrated with an asset schedule where intangible rises while R&D output is absent. Sign three is inflated assets via related-party loans or inventory that never moves, a table shows inventory days at 200 where industry is 30 and auditor notes advance to supplier from promoter entity.

Sign four is hidden liabilities via contingent guarantees or off-balance subsidiary debt, shown as a guarantee footnote at 80 percent of net worth where collapse would wipe equity. Sign five is inconsistent depreciation versus gross block where asset age rises but depreciation falls to boost profit, a chart plots depreciation rate declining while gross block ages. Sign six is frequent auditor or policy changes, a timeline shows three auditors in four years before a restatement, a classic tell. Sign seven is promoter pledge and share issuance that recycles equity to mask leverage, illustrated as pledge rising from 10 to 60 percent while promoter holding falls, funding personal ventures.

Malik recounts catching each sign live: a textile firm where other income from asset sale made net profit positive despite operating loss, and a construction firm where contingent liabilities were three times equity before bank invocation. The chapter gives a one-page shenanigan checklist with thresholds: receivable growth not exceed 1.2 times sales growth, other income below 20 percent of PBT, pledge below 20 percent, auditor tenure at least three years. The illustration that readers photocopy is a red-flag dashboard where each sign is green or red, and any two reds is automatic avoid regardless of valuation.

The closing reminder is that cooking is rarely one sign; frauds cluster at least three, so breadth of flags matters more than magnitude of one, and peace comes from eliminating seventy percent of screen survivors here before valuation temptation arises. chapters.title: How to Do Valuation Analysis of a Company
chapters.summary:
Valuation is presented as margin of safety arithmetic, not price prediction, and Malik is explicit that earnings yield must cover risks that business and forensic checks cannot eliminate. He starts with earnings yield where yield equals PAT divided by market cap, the inverse of P-E, and compares it to bank fixed deposit plus risk premium. A table shows Asian Paints at P-E 40 yields 2.5 percent versus HDFC deposit at 8 percent, so the market is paying for growth at 15 percent that must materialize, illustrated as a hurdle rate bridge.

Next is discounted cash flow stripped to essentials: project FCF for five years at self-sustainable growth, terminal at nominal GDP, discount at ten to twelve percent for equity risk, and derive intrinsic value with sensitivity tornado chart where growth plus or minus two points swings value thirty percent, teaching humility. Malik warns against garbage-in gospel-out where aggressive growth assumptions justify any price; he caps growth at historical ROCE times retention and never above nominal GDP plus three points. The hidden risk of high P-E stocks chapter is previewed with a valuation versus quality matrix: high quality at high P-E can still be poor if growth disappoints, illustrated as a two-by-two where high quality high price is losers when earnings miss.

An anecdote recounts buying a high P-E midcap at 50 times after forensic green, then suffering sixty percent drawdown when growth slipped from thirty to fifteen percent, a P-E compression chart shows multiple halving. The low P-E opportunity is framed contrarily: a dull stock at P-E 10 with fifteen percent ROCE and visible growth can yield twenty percent if market re-rates to 15 times, a scenarios table shows re-rating plus growth compounding. Malik also covers earnings yield plus growth as quick check — if yield plus growth exceeds FD plus six percent, there is compensation.

The chapter's valuation checklist asks: is earnings yield plus sustainable growth at least double government bond, does DCF margin of safety exceed thirty percent at conservative growth, and is promoter buying alongside you via open market purchases reported to exchanges. The closing illustration is a valuation traffic light where green requires both forensic and business gates passed plus margin of safety green; yellow is hold, red is avoid irrespective of story quality, reinforcing that peace requires price discipline after quality confirmation. chapters.title: Business & Industry Analysis and Management Assessment
chapters.summary:
The final section condenses industry economics and promoter quality, which Malik calls most critical factor despite being last. Business and industry analysis asks whether the funnel is widening: unorganized to organized share, per capita penetration, and regulatory tailwind. A penetration chart shows pipes per household India at 0.3 versus China 1.2, justifying Astral runway. Porter's five forces are sketched quickly: buyer power is high when top five customers exceed thirty percent of sales, supplier power high when single resin supplier, and Malik shows Astral mitigates supplier by exclusive Lubrizol but pays royalty — a trade-off. The crucial insight slides show industry P-E relevance is conditional: paying industry median multiple only makes sense if the firm's ROCE exceeds median; a scatter plots ROCE versus P-E where outliers above trend are attractive.

Management assessment, covered in three parts, is reduced to observable proxies because meeting promoters is often PR. Part one checks integrity via related-party cleanliness, auditor tenure, and tax disputes where contested tax exceeding twenty percent of profit signals aggressiveness, illustrated with a tax contingency table. Part two checks capital allocation: does capex go to core ROCE-accretive plants or into unrelated hotels and power, a capex allocation pie reveals drift. Part three checks governance via board independence and remuneration where promoter pay rising faster than ROCE is extraction, shown as diverging lines. Anecdotes include a promoter who took zero dividend but salary at ten percent of profit, and another who issued warrants to himself at thirty percent discount, both failing checklist.

The illustration that anchors the chapter is the final buy checklist page 181 where business, financial, valuation, and management each have green ticks before buy; any red in management is veto even if financials shine, because integrity cannot be outsourced. The closing selects three guidelines for retail: own eight to twelve stocks not fifty, monitor quarterly results only for thesis break not price, and sell when management breaks trust or debt funds growth beyond self-sustainable rate. A portfolio monitoring table last chapter shows Malik's own holdings with thesis and red-flag tracking, proving peaceful investing is a practice of quarterly checklist maintenance, not daily ticker watching. The book ends with premium services disclaimer and the quiet promise that peace is the return you keep when other returns fluctuate.

takeaways: Prefer widening funnels where per capita penetration and unorganized share still leave runway.
Require firm's ROCE above industry median before paying industry P-E; otherwise you overpay for mediocrity.
Veto any business where management extracts pay faster than ROCE or routes capex to unrelated ventures.
